hero.name: Tarun
hero.who: a 27-year-old bank officer in Indore who dreams of selling handloom bedsheets

story.b: Tarun works at a bank branch in Indore, checking loan files from ten to six. His father is proud of the job. But Tarun cannot stop thinking about the handloom cotton bedsheets his grandmother used to buy from weavers in Maheshwar, soft as old kurtas and lasting for years. Most city shops now sell cheap printed sheets that fade in months. He imagines a small brand that brings the weavers' work to homes in Mumbai and Bengaluru. Every night after dinner, he sketches ideas in a diary. When he mentions it at home, his father laughs and his mother worries aloud about marriage proposals. His friends call it a hobby. Tarun lies awake, unable to let it go.

ask.q: Everyone calls Tarun's idea silly, but he cannot stop thinking about it. What should he do?
o: Quit his job tomorrow and put all his savings into it
Forget it and listen to his family, since they know best
Give the idea a serious, small test while staying practical
ask.why: An idea that refuses to leave you deserves a real test, even if others call it silly. Dropping it means never knowing. Quitting at once and betting all his savings ignores the risk. A small, practical test lets him believe in the idea and still protect himself.

chapters.take: If an idea will not leave you alone, give it a serious test.

story.b: Tarun takes a week of leave and rides the bus to Maheshwar. He spends two days with a weaver family, the Ansaris, drinking tea on their porch while the looms clatter. He buys thirty bedsheets with his own savings, photographs them on his terrace in the morning light and posts them online with simple stories about who wove each one. All thirty sell in ten days, mostly to strangers. Something in his chest lifts. He writes the idea in one sentence and reads it to his mother: real handloom sheets, straight from weavers, for city homes. She does not laugh this time. Now Tarun has to decide whether to leave the bank.

ask.q: Tarun's first thirty sheets sold fast. How should he decide about leaving his bank job?
o: Quit with enough savings for several months and a clear plan to return if needed
Stay at the bank forever, since one good batch proves nothing
Quit at once and borrow from relatives to order a thousand sheets
ask.why: A crazy idea is worth following when there is a real sign it works, and staying practical protects him while he learns. Staying forever ignores the clear early signal. Borrowing heavily for a giant order turns one good week into a huge bet.

chapters.take: Follow the idea you believe in, but keep one foot on solid ground.

story.h: The big order and the empty account
story.b: Eight months after leaving the bank, Tarun gets the order of his dreams. A chain of home stores in Mumbai wants two thousand bedsheets. He celebrates with his cousin Neha over poha and jalebi at Sarafa. Then the numbers hit him. The weavers need payment for yarn and labour before they start. The store will pay him ninety days after delivery. Sales are booming, but his bank account is nearly empty. The bank manager, his old colleague, gets nervous when Tarun asks for a bigger loan. For the first time, Tarun opens a simple sheet and writes down every rupee coming in and going out, week by week, for the next four months. The gap is frightening.

ask.q: Tarun's sales are booming but cash is running out before the store pays. What should he do?
o: Accept even more orders, since higher sales will solve everything
Track cash weekly and negotiate part payment upfront before committing
Stop paying the weavers on time until the store pays him
ask.why: A growing business needs cash for stock and labour long before customers pay, so sales alone can sink it. Watching cash closely and asking for part payment protects the business. More orders deepen the gap, and delaying the weavers hurts the people his brand depends on.

chapters.take: Growth needs cash before it brings cash. Watch cash as closely as sales.

story.b: Tarun cannot do everything alone anymore. He interviews a polished business graduate who talks smoothly about scaling but asks mostly about salary and weekends off. Then he meets three very different people. His cousin Neha left a fashion course halfway but can spot a loose thread across a room. Bablu spent ten years dispatching trucks from Indore's transport hub and knows every courier route by heart. Mrs Dubey, a retired maths teacher from Tarun's old school, offers to keep the accounts and checks every rupee twice. None of them look impressive on paper. All of them light up when they touch the sheets and hear about the weavers. Tarun has to choose.

ask.q: Tarun must choose between a polished graduate and three unusual people who love the mission. What should guide his choice?
o: Hire the graduate, since a strong resume always means strong results
Hire no one and keep doing every job himself
Hire people who care about the mission and bring different strengths
ask.why: In a fragile young company, passion, trust and different skills often matter more than a perfect resume. People who care deeply will push through the hard months. A polished hire focused on salary may leave at the first crisis, and doing everything alone will burn Tarun out.

chapters.take: In a young company, care and trust can beat a perfect resume.

story.b: In July, two things go wrong in the same week. The Mumbai store chain, which now buys most of Tarun's sheets, says it is cutting orders by half to try a cheaper supplier. And heavy rain damages two looms at the Ansaris' workshop, the only weavers Tarun works with. For a few days the whole business wobbles. Mrs Dubey shows him the numbers without softening them. Tarun realises he has built his company on two single threads. Once the panic settles, he travels to meet weaver families in Chanderi and a cooperative near Maheshwar, and Neha starts building their own website so more sales come straight from customers instead of one big buyer.

ask.q: Tarun's business depends on one big buyer and one weaver family. What should he do?
o: Build backups, like more weaver partners and his own direct sales
Offer the chain a deep discount so it never leaves
Wait patiently, since good partners usually come back
ask.why: Relying on a single buyer or supplier means one broken relationship can shake the whole business. Adding weaver partners and selling directly spreads the risk and gives him more control. A deep discount ties him even tighter to one buyer, and waiting leaves everything to luck.

chapters.take: If one partner can sink you, build a backup before you need it.

story.b: Two years in, the business is finally stable. But one evening, scrolling through his phone in a Delhi hotel after a trade fair, Tarun sees photos of his sister Ritu's engagement ceremony back home. He had promised to come and then stayed back for one more buyer meeting. His father is smiling in the photos, but he looks thinner than Tarun remembers. Tarun realises he has not eaten dinner with his parents in months. The company has taken his evenings, his Sundays and his calls home, one small yes at a time. Nobody forced him. On the flight back, he opens his calendar and blocks every Sunday evening, marked simply family, phone off.

ask.q: Tarun's business is growing, but he keeps missing family moments. What should he do?
o: Push through for a few more years and make it up to them later
Protect regular offline time with family, starting this week
Send expensive gifts to show he still cares
ask.why: Ambition can quietly take years that never come back, one small yes at a time. Blocking regular family time now protects what matters most. Later often never comes, and gifts cannot replace being present at the dinner table or at a sister's engagement.

chapters.take: Building something big is worth it only if the people you love still get you.

story.b: Three years after leaving the bank, Tarun's brand works with five weaver families and a cooperative across two towns. The website now brings in more than half the sales, and no single buyer can shake the business anymore. Mrs Dubey still checks every rupee twice, and the cash sheet is updated every Monday morning before anything else. Bablu has trained two new dispatch helpers. Neha designed a new range in indigo that sold out in a month. On Sunday evenings, Tarun's phone stays in a drawer. He sits with his parents on the terrace, eating his mother's dal bafla, while his father tells the neighbours, a little too loudly, that his son makes bedsheets for half of India.

chapters.take: A lasting business needs belief, cash, good people and time for those you love.
